item.title: The Duty of a Scholar (125 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.daemonology.net/blog/2026-10-31-The-Duty-of-a-Scholar.html, See on Hacker News

On November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state.

There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly.

This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. As it turned out, being unemployed proved useful in early May, when Intel — rather irked by my impending publication — asked Yahoo to order me to withdraw the paper; Yahoo was very happy to reply that, unlike many FreeBSD developers, I was not in fact employed by them and they were not in a position to threaten to fire me. On May 13th, 2005, I presented my paper at BSDCan and published an advisory on the topic; advisories were published at the same time or soon thereafter by FreeBSD, NetBSD, Red Hat, SCO, and Ubuntu.

Anyone involved with open source software security will recognize the process of responsible disclosure (now widely called "coordinated disclosure", after some people in the industry struggled with the concept of responsibility), although the length of this particular process was unusual. If you find a security vulnerability, you shouldn't ignore it (or worse, sell it to bad actors); conversely, it's irresponsible to simply publish the vulnerability and hope that the good guys can fix it before the bad guys exploit it. Instead, you have a responsibility to identify who needs to know about the issue and to contact them — quietly — so they can get patches ready to distribute to their users the moment the issue becomes publicly known.

In this particular case, I was unusually able to put my life on hold: I was single, child-free, and, after defending my thesis and returning home to Canada, living rent-free in my (very tolerant) parents' basement. While I had some bills to cover — being a type 1 diabetic, I had to purchase insulin — living in Canada meant that I didn't need to worry about the risk of extraordinary costs from a hospital stay. Had I been living in the USA, I would have needed to prioritize seeking employment and medical insurance and likely would not have been able to discharge the duty which fate had thrust upon me.

Engineers, of course, are familiar with such duties: While the precise language varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, nearly all professional ethical codes include a requirement to act upon safety hazards regardless of whether any personal connection exists. Members of the IEEE commit, for example, "to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public..." without that duty being limited to hazards arising from projects employing the Engineer in question: The duty "to disclose promptly" vests in any Engineer who recognizes that the hazard exists. As with responsible disclosure of software security vulnerabilities, however, the subject matter of this duty is limited in scope: There is no duty to report if work is being done inefficiently. As a legal duty this would be reasonable; but as a moral duty, I feel it sets the bar too low.

Engineering codes also often set out a process of escalation: In the common case of a licensed Engineer becoming aware of a hazard in a project they are working on, in the first instance they should report their concerns to their employer; only if that fails to yield results should they take more direct steps. This is both efficient and practical: Reporting an issue to someone who fails to act upon it isn't necessarily sufficient to discharge a duty, but conversely reporting everything broadly risks drowning out the few items which truly need broad attention. I routinely apply this same principle; for example, in 2009 I discovered that the Amazon EC2 firewall broke Path MTU Discovery by default and reported it to Amazon; but by November 2012 I concluded that Amazon was not going to address the problem, so I took to my blog to advise Amazon customers on how to fix Path MTU Discovery for themselves. (As it happened, Amazon fixed the bug a short time later.) While this was in no way a safety or computer security concern, I felt that, knowing what I did, I had an ethical duty to share that knowledge to help people who were affected by the issue.

In the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode "The First Duty", the late Patrick Stewart, speaking as Jean-Luc Picard, delivers a memorable speech about truth:

The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it's scientific truth or historical truth or personal truth! It is the guiding principle on which Starfleet is based! If you can't find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don't deserve to wear that uniform!

The duty described here is a duty to uncover and not conceal the truth; while I agree with this duty, I don't think it goes far enough. To me, the duty includes actively seeking out people to whom the truth should be told. To hide behind "nobody asked" is to fail to fulfill the duty.

Much ink has been spilled by philosophers about duty and ethics, and the German Enlightenment philosopher Fichte in particular had some interesting comments to make in the fourth of his 1794 lectures, Über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten — often translated as The Vocation of the Scholar, which inspired the title of this essay. Fichte argues that Scholars have a particular relationship to knowledge: A Scholar "possesses his Knowledge not for himself, but for society". It is not proper for a Scholar to hoard knowledge; rather, Scholars have a duty to impart their knowledge to others — in Fichte's somewhat exaggerated view, to act as "the Teacher of the human race". On the other hand, it is unnecessary and inappropriate to enter with everyone into the "deep inquiries which he himself has been obliged to undertake"; rather, a Scholar relies upon others' trust in the Scholar's honesty when conveying the particular knowledge which is needed. Fichte notes that "[t]he Scholar will never be tempted to bring men to the adoption of his convictions by coercion or the use of physical force [...] neither will he deceive them". Scholars are not Plato's philosopher-kings; their duty is to provide the requisite knowledge, not to enforce what is done with that knowledge.

Now, I don't agree with Fichte on every point. Fichte considers Scholars to be the loftiest of all classes, and even invites each Scholar to consider themselves a "Priest of Truth"; living in rather more egalitarian times, I absolutely reject this framing. Nor do I accept Fichte's framing (in his preceding lecture, On the Distinction of Classes in Society) that the duty of Scholars to share knowledge arises from an obligation to render back to society what it has done for us; to me, the duty arises not from a debt to society, but rather attaches to knowledge itself, no matter who holds it.

This duty, naturally, is not unlimited. As Fichte notes, there is no duty to force people to act upon shared knowledge — indeed there is a moral obligation to accept everyone's freedom to choose how they act. Similarly, there is no duty to become a Cassandra: As with any gift, people are free to refuse the gift of knowledge, however unwise that might be; ultimately, if everyone who is able to act upon some knowledge has been made aware of it, the duty has been exhausted.

In modern vernacular, the terms "Scholar" and "Researcher" often overlap, but to me there is a very precise distinction: Researchers create new knowledge, while Scholars carry that knowledge to the people who need it — a narrower definition than that of Fichte, whose Scholars also carry a duty to strive to extend knowledge. Many people, of course, are both Researchers and Scholars; but there are plenty of people who perform research and publish papers without truly communicating their discoveries. The research paper which is published in a journal but never read is almost a cliché; but even papers which are read do not necessarily have the impact they deserve if they are read only by academics and not by anyone in a position to act upon the findings published. My undergraduate alma mater, Simon Fraser University — of which I have been a sitting Senator for over two decades — describes itself as "Canada's engaged university" and makes a point of valuing not just academic output but the work of connecting academic learning with the real world. A true Scholar, in my mind, is someone who feels bound by the duty of knowledge: To find the people with whom it should be shared.

It is for everyone to choose their own role in society, and not everyone feels every duty the same way; for that matter, just as my experience in 2005 would have been different had I needed to obtain medical insurance, not everyone is able to act upon a duty, no matter how much they feel it. But for myself, I choose the life and duty of a Scholar.

item.title: It's the memory latency, stupid (213 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://pivotlake.io/blog/its-the-memory-latency-stupid/, See on Hacker News

When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%?

The answer is usually memory.

Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM.

Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering.

Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses.

To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity:

fn consume(
    &mut self,
    batch: RecordBatch,
    _sender: &mut dyn Sender<RecordBatch>,
) -> unary::Result<()> {
    let group_keys = batch.column(self.key_column).as_primitive::<Int64Type>();
    for &key in group_keys.values() {
        // If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0
        // Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column
        *self.counts.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
}

We'll then run a simple query SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per UserID, meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per UserID- I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique UserID.
Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores.

To run it:

cat > config.yaml <<'EOF'
server:
  bind: 127.0.0.1:5440
workers: 1
datastores:
  default:
    kind: pivotlake
    location: ./data
    default: true
users:
  pivot:
    auth:
      method: trust
EOF
taskset -c 3 pivot server --config config.yaml &
taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache.

You'll notice we did taskset -c. This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run perf stat on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op:

sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

and we get back this

Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        8364109137      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     50.1 %  backend_bound_memory
       38233214040      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        8977647849      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       11861387798      ls_not_halted_cyc
       11431618219      ex_ret_ops                       #     16.1 %  retiring
       11858248045      ls_not_halted_cyc

       4.030148989 seconds time elapsed

This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations.

Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches):

sudo perf stat -C 3   -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

And the result:

 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          76190837      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.996301634 seconds time elapsed

Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching).

Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases:

Phase 1: In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096).

fn consume(
    &mut self,
    batch: RecordBatch,
    _sender: &mut dyn Sender<RecordBatch>,
) -> unary::Result<()> {
    let keys = batch.column(self.key_column).as_primitive::<Int64Type>();
    for &key in keys.values() {
        let hash = self.hasher.hash_one(key);
        // Since we want top 12 bits, we shift the hash (a u64) 52 bits to the right
        let partition = (hash >> 52) as usize;
        self.partitions[partition].push(&mut self.allocator, (hash, key));
    }
    Ok(())
}

Phase 2: When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1.

fn into_outputter(self) -> unary::Result<Option<Self::Outputter>> {
    let mut groups = Vec::new();
    for rows in &self.partitions {
        let mut table: HashTable<(u64, i64, u64)> = HashTable::new();   // (hash, key, count)
        rows.for_each(|(hash, key)| {
            match table.entry(hash, |group| group.1 == key, |group| group.0) {
                Entry::Occupied(mut group) => group.get_mut().2 += 1,
                Entry::Vacant(slot) => { slot.insert((hash, key, 1)); }
            }
        });
        groups.extend(table.into_iter().map(|(_, key, count)| (key, count)));
    }
    Ok(Some(Outputter::new(groups)))
}

At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing more operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs.

The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps smaller. By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it!

taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again:

sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"

And our results:

 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        3790955223      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     23.5 %  backend_bound_memory
       20376118172      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        5442424751      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       10083617764      ls_not_halted_cyc
       19350459182      ex_ret_ops                       #     32.2 %  retiring
       10023435553      ls_not_halted_cyc

       3.575992317 seconds time elapsed

Now we can see the picture has completely changed- 23.5% of the time is spent on waiting for memory (as opposed to 50% before), 32% for actually retiring operations. You may notice we're actually doing more work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the ex_ret_ops counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. This is worth it though, because as we said before- if we can translate cold DRAM accesses into CPU instructions, it's nearly always a good trade to make. In this case, we went down from 8364109137 CPU slots stalled because of memory to 3790955223.

To complete the picture and really see we're pulling less memory from the DRAM, let's again check how many our memory loads come from DRAM:

sudo perf stat -C 3   -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          25688280      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.009547012 seconds time elapsed

Whoo! That means that on demand we pulled 1.5GB from DRAM, instead of 4.5GB in the naive version.

That, of course, isn't the limit of how much we can utilize our CPU cache for GROUP BYs. And utilizing our CPU cache isn't the only way we can "hide" DRAM latency; another trick is prefetching memory to our cache before we need it, and yet another trick is creating algorithms that allow maximization of memory throughput- but that's not for this blog! We'll go into that in our next blog where we look at our /seemingly very weird/ implementation of JOIN probing.

For now, without explaining too much, I'll leave you with Pivot's speed for this query on a single core:

Time: 1848.353 ms (00:01.848)

and the amount of RAM we bring:

 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          14917958      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       2.182674864 seconds time elapsed

Which comes out to 954 MB.

Of course, Pivot knows to run in parallel on our 16 cores (where there are many other interesting cases), in which case it comes out to:

nice :)

Try out Pivot if you want to have super speeds above parquets (OSS fun!), see you next time.

item.title: UK Green party drops longstanding opposition to nuclear power (214 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/oct/05/green-party-nuclear-power-policy, See on Hacker News

Green party members have voted to end the party’s opposition to nuclear power, dropping a commitment to phase out the technology in a major shift in its energy policy.

The motion, adopted at conference, removes a “blanket opposition to nuclear fission” and instead commits the Green party of England and Wales to assessing nuclear projects alongside other low-carbon technologies.

Its electricity generation policy still prioritises offshore wind, onshore wind and rooftop solar as the primary sources of electricity, but allows elected representatives to support new nuclear reactors on a case-by-case basis.

The Green MP Carla Denyer said the decision recognised there was a role for nuclear while the country moved towards an electricity system based primarily on renewables. “This evolution of our policy does not commit the party to backing new nuclear, but accepts this power source is here to stay for now, while we transition to electricity generation based primarily on renewable sources,” she said.

Denyer said keeping existing nuclear stations running could be a low-carbon option because a significant proportion of their carbon footprint came from construction. “So if I were energy secretary, my evidence-based approach would be to keep existing nuclear plants in operation, but to consider proposals for new nuclear power very carefully, bearing in mind the cost, speed and environmental impacts.”

Her comments strike a different tone from her assessment in 2023, when she described nuclear energy as “incredibly slow and incredibly expensive”. She said at the time: “Renewables is simply the way forward. Nuclear is not going to help us out in this climate emergency.”

Other senior Greens have previously criticised the technology. The party’s leader, Zack Polanski, has described it as outdated and compared investment in new nuclear reactors to “creating a fax machine”.

Last year, Adrian Ramsay, then a Green co-leader, criticised government support for Sizewell C. “The money being spent on this nuclear gamble would be far better spent on insulating and retrofitting millions of homes, bringing down energy bills and keeping people warmer and more comfortable,” he said.

The Green’s previous opposition to nuclear fission was rooted in its staunch opposition of nuclear weapons, one of the party’s founding principles.

Eugene McCarthy, a co-founder of Greens for Nuclear and a supporter of the motion, said the urgency of the climate crisis demanded a willingness to consider all available options. “We are at the throw-the-kitchen-sink-at-it phase of the climate crisis where you cannot be ruling anything out for things like Chernobyl happening in the 1980s,” he said.

The motion allows elected representatives to assess individual proposals on their merits, McCarthy said. “We will not say we support or don’t support any particular technology. This motion basically lets our elected members of parliament take it on a case-by-case basis and go: ‘This makes sense, we will extend the lifetime of Sizewell B,’ and on a different case say: ‘Actually the numbers don’t add up here.’”

Asked about Polanski’s previous criticism of nuclear, McCarthy said the leader remained entitled to his views. “He’s still fully entitled to say that, and a lot of the nuclear technology that we are using is quite outdated, to be frank. What this means is that he can now take a nuanced position.”

Prof Andrew Stirling, who has advised government on nuclear power and energy policy, said the motion was “completely irrational”. “Why would a party that pioneered concerns about nuclear power that have been so broadly vindicated by history, choose now to shift its position?” he said.

“All authoritative sources agree that climate action is much faster, affordable and impactful with combined renewables and storage,” he added. “Why spend scarce resources on less effective actions?”

McCarthy said: “Renewables are cheaper and have much more capacity, and you can roll them out much quicker. [But] there are issues with baseload, which nuclear can help with.”

item.title: Malware uses LLMs to rank victims by how much they're worth (249 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/appraisal-by-ai-model-driven-victim-prioritization-in-the-volta-infostealer/, See on Hacker News

Saturday, October 31, 2026 08:00

  • VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.
  • If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. 
  • This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. 

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort, is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.” 

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions 

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 

moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash 

0.2 — deterministic, consistent output 

Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

Stealer capabilities 

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.  

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated. 

Deployment model 

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.  

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.  

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.  

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

Countermeasures 

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. 

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. 

Conclusions 

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM, though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement. 

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

item.title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4 (274 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://jepsen.io/analyses/particledb-1.1.4, See on Hacker News

ParticleDB is a multi-model database designed for AI workloads. We tested versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 and found that ParticleDB’s claims of “Full ACID” were somewhat premature. We present 96 issues in ParticleDB, ranging from the pedestrian (crashes, deadlocks, data loss, etc.) to the piquant (partially-invisible rows which could not be deleted, WHERE 4 = 5, dropped tables re-emerging in distorted forms, confused columns, strings turning into integers, and so on). Most issues required just a single server, single client, and no faults. By version 1.1.18.11.rc-22, all but ten of those issues appeared resolved. However, ParticleDB continued to lose committed writes during normal operation with the default occ transaction mode, and allowed internal anomalies and Lost Update with serializable, the strongest setting. Orkes, the makers of ParticleDB, have since released version 1.1.19-rc.13; they claim that it resolves all remaining issues discussed in this report. This research was funded by Orkes, Inc., and conducted in accordance with the Jepsen ethics policy.

Background

Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems: databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on. Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate systems remains an open research problem.

ParticleDB1 aims to unify these workloads in a single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live analytics, and user-defined functions called Particles.2 To integrate with existing systems, clients can connect through a variety of interfaces, including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust, ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the same safety characteristics.

ParticleDB was built by Orkes to support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor. Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database. ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run 1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai. Orkes engaged Jepsen to test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4.

While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a replicated cluster using the Raft consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior.

Safety

ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.

ParticleDB offered three tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The sync mode called fsync on each commit, groupsync batched multiple transactions into a single fsync, and nosync skipped fsync altogether. The Transaction Engine documentation described sync as offering “stronger durability” than groupsync. On the other hand, particledb start --help said the groupsync mode ensured that “COMMIT waits for flush”, and Orkes’ internal operator guide concurred: groupsync offered the “same durability as sync”.

ParticleDB’s home page proudly claimed “Full ACID. 159K TPS.” However, the text immediately below this said “snapshot isolation”, which is not fully isolated.

Most SQL databases use the SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL statement to control the concurrent semantics of a transaction. However, ParticleDB ignored or rejected these statements. In some cases it instructed users to choose READ COMMITTED, a relatively weak isolation level. In other cases it accepted requests for different isolation levels, and silently ignored them (despite documentation to the contrary).

Instead, transaction isolation was governed by the --txn-mode setting passed at startup. The transaction engine documentation described four modes:

Mode Behavior When to use
fast No locks; commit-on-write Bulk loads, single-writer benchmarks
occ Overlay + commit-time OCC validation (default) General OLTP — safe under concurrency
zero-copy-occ Partition-pinned OCC; single-partition txns skip cross-partition coordination High-throughput OLTP on partition-affine workloads (TPC-C, key-value)
table-2pl Exclusive table locks at first touch Strictest serialization, simple semantics

This table was difficult to interpret. While the best practices documentation warned that users should “pick --txn-mode deliberately”, since “it changes correctness and throughput characteristics more than SQL text does”, the documentation did not explain what these modes actually guaranteed. The fast mode was clearly intended for weaker isolation, but was that Read Atomic, Read Uncommitted, or something else? The occ mode was similarly unclear. “Commit-time OCC validation” could describe a broad spectrum of consistency models from Read Uncommitted to Strong Serializable, but “safe under concurrency” suggests it might be Serializable. The zero-copy-occ mode described a performance optimization which could be as safe as occ, but it was not described as “safe under concurrency”—raising the question: in what ways was it unsafe? Finally, if table-2pl offered the “strictest serialization”, was occ some weaker isolation level?

The CLI reference page contained another table which described occ and table-2pl as “Jepsen-safe”, whereas fast was not “Jepsen-safe”, but did not explain their safety properties. Since Jepsen evaluates safety with respect to documentation and marketing claims, it is not clear how to interpret these terms.3

Running particledb start --help provided the following table:

Mode Description
fast No locks, maximum OLTP throughput (unsafe under concurrency)
occ Table locks + commit-time validation (safe for most OLTP)
row-2pl Alias for occ
zero-copy-occ Partition-pinned OCC (highest throughput safe mode)
table-2pl Exclusive table locks, full serialization (strictest)
serializable Alias for table-2pl
serializable-ssi Adaptive SSI (Cahill 2008), PL-3 with optimistic semantics (v1 scaffolding — see SSI_ADAPTIVE_DESIGN.md)

The point of Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is generally to avoid taking locks, so the mention of table locks and a row-2pl4 alias was surprising. Moreover, “safe for most OLTP” undermines the claim that occ was “safe under concurrency”; it suggests there are some OLTP workloads which are unsafe!

Orkes explained that this documentation was wrong: occ was actually optimistic, and the row-2pl alias was to preserve compatibility with an earlier two-phase locking mechanism. They also provided an unpublished operator guide with detailed descriptions of the various transaction modes. This document was difficult to interpret, but did specify the following consistency models:

Mode Consistency Model
fast Unknown
occ-v3 (a.k.a. occ, occ-v2, row-2pl) Snapshot Isolation
zero-copy-occ (a.k.a. zocc) Snapshot Isolation
serializable-ssi (a.k.a. ssi) Serializable
table-2pl (a.k.a. serializable) Strong Serializable

Sources disagreed about the default transaction and WAL sync modes, but in general, occ-v3 and groupsync appeared to be the default.

Test Design

We wrote a test suite for ParticleDB using the Jepsen testing library. We ran ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 on individual Debian 13 nodes, both in containers and EC2 VMs. Our test harness could simulate process crashes by killing ParticleDB, simulate the loss of un-fsynced writes using LazyFS, and truncate or corrupt disk files. We ran ParticleDB using each transaction mode and all three WAL sync modes.

We first tried ParticleDB’s official Java SDK. While the documentation indicated that the library was available as a Maven dependency, neither the JAR nor source code were actually available. Instead, we began with the official Postgres JDBC client, version 42.7.11, and later added support for the ParticleDB Java SDK, versions 1.0.0 through 1.0.2.

Workloads

We used several Jepsen workloads from other SQL databases, and designed new ones specifically for ParticleDB.

The rw workload performed randomly generated transactions involving reads and writes of integer values identified by unique integer keys. We stored each value in a single row and accessed them both via primary and unindexed secondary keys. Keys and values were encoded as a variety of datatypes, including integers, decimals, and strings. We assumed that writes followed reads within each transaction, and that individual keys were sequentially consistent, and used these assumptions to infer constraints on the version orders and transaction dependency graphs. Jepsen’s transactional checker, Elle, then searched for cycles in that dependency graph, as well as a variety of non-cyclic phenomena like G1a (Aborted Read).

The append workload also performed randomly generated transactions over rows identified by unique integer keys, but the values were lists of integers. Transactions could read one of these lists by key, or append a unique integer to a list by key. We encoded each list as a comma-separated text field, and used SQL concat to append to them. Rows could be selected via primary key or unindexed secondary key, or via a join to an indirection table. From there, we used Elle to infer version orders and dependency graphs, and searched for a variety of cyclic and non-cyclic phenomena.

When these workloads revealed consistency violations within a single transaction, we designed an internal workload to stress internal consistency. This workload performed a series of randomly generated transactions involving INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT statements over a simple key-value table, and verified that within each individual transaction, reads observed prior writes.

To investigate tantalizing anomalies in the internal workload, we designed the compare workload. This workload used Clojure’s test.check generative testing library to produce random tables and simple SQL statements over them, then executed those statements against both ParticleDB and PostgreSQL. If ParticleDB’s behavior was not equivalent to PostgreSQL’s, the compare workload would search for a simpler sequence of statements that could reproduce the same divergence. Although our SQL generator was relatively simple—just a few basic datatypes, literals, arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic, transactions, and some simple LIMIT, OFFSET, and ORDER BY clauses—it proved remarkably fruitful.

Drawing on these successes, we devised a hybrid internal-sim workload to search for violations of internal consistency in more complex transactions. This workload generated a random set of tables, then concurrently executed random transactions over them. It then checked each transaction independently to ensure that each of its statements observed results consistent with those preceding. For example, if a transaction executed DELETE ... WHERE 2 < c, then observed a row with c = 3, we could prove that transaction was not internally consistent.
